routes.title: DECISION 1: HOW WILL YOUR DATA TRAVEL?
routes.intro: Spirit and Opportunity had two ways to send data home:

lines.text: > DIRECT-TO-EARTH (X-band): the rover points its antenna at Earth and talks to NASA's Deep Space Network. No orbiter needed, but the link is slower and uses more of the rover's energy.*
> UHF RELAY: the rover sends data up to an orbiter like Mars Odyssey, which forwards it to Earth. Rates up to 128 kbps, but only while the orbiter passes overhead.

fact.text: By the end of the prime mission (April 2004), 89% of the rovers' data had come home through UHF relays.

routes.mentor: Your rover has both antennas installed, so both routes are possible. Think about speed, energy and timing!

windows.title: DECISION 2: WHEN CAN YOU TALK?
windows.intro: A Martian day (a sol) lasts about 24.6 hours. Contacts only happen in short windows:

lines.text: > ORBITER PASSES: Odyssey or Mars Global Surveyor fly over the rover for only 2 to 8 minutes. A pass high in the sky gives a stronger link than a low one.
> DIRECT-TO-EARTH: possible only while Earth is above the rover's horizon and a Deep Space Network antenna is free.*
> NIGHT CONTACTS: in this game, waking up in the cold night costs extra battery energy.*

windows.formula: Window length x link speed = how much data you can send.
windows.mentor: A longer pass is not always better if it costs energy your rover needs to survive the night.

priority.title: DECISION 3: WHAT GOES FIRST?
priority.intro: Your rover collected more data than one pass can carry. You must choose the order.

lines.text: > ROVER TELEMETRY: a small health report. Without it, the team on Earth can't know if the rover is safe.
> ANALYSIS RESULTS: small files from spectrometers. They hold the strongest evidence of ancient water.
> IMAGES: close-ups and panoramas are huge. They help explain the evidence, but fill the link quickly.

priority.rule: Send the most valuable and smallest science first.
priority.mentor: Real teams decided every sol which data came down first. Science and rover safety both matter!

routes.name: A. DIRECT-TO-EARTH (X-BAND)
routes.needs: Earth above the horizon + DSN antenna

feedback.smallFirst: + Small, high-value results first: the key water evidence made it home in one pass.
feedback.scienceLate: - The key water evidence did not make it into this pass. Put small, valuable results higher.
feedback.telemetryFirst: + Telemetry first lets the team check that the rover is healthy.
feedback.telemetryLate: - Telemetry was not first: the team can't check the rover's health right away.
feedback.partial: - {NAME} did not fully fit. A second pass (or the night pass, at an energy cost) could finish it.
feedback.dteNote: i The direct X-band route would have returned about 36 Mb* using more energy.
feedback.uhfNote: i The UHF relay route could have returned about 60 Mb* using less energy.
feedback.night: - The night pass worked, but the cold wake-up cost a lot of battery.*
feedback.good: Great plan! Spirit and Opportunity sent most of their science through orbiters, just like you. Now let's actually send it!
feedback.ok: Good plan, with room to improve. Most real MER data came home through orbiter relays. Now let's send it!

cards.title: 1. LIGHT DELAY
cards.text: Radio travels at the speed of light, but Mars is so far away that a message takes about 3 to 22 minutes one way. Nobody can drive the rover with a joystick!

cards.title: 2. RELAY ORBITERS
cards.text: Spirit and Opportunity sent most of their data through orbiters like Mars Odyssey. An orbiter passes overhead for only 2 to 8 minutes, so timing matters.

cards.title: 3. THREE BIG DISHES
cards.text: NASA's Deep Space Network has three antenna complexes, about 120° apart around the world: California, Spain and Australia, so the network can keep talking to spacecraft as Earth turns.
